story: A Mexican one peso from 1975, carrying Jose Maria Morelos, the priest who became a general of Mexico's independence war and was executed for it in 1815. His portrait faces left under the words UN PESO; the other side shows Mexico's national emblem, the eagle with a snake in its beak standing on a cactus — the sign the Aztecs were told to look for when founding their city. Mexico struck this peso, in copper-nickel, through the 1970s and into the early 1980s, and it jingled in every pocket and bus fare in the country. The little Mo beside the portrait is the Mexico City mint's mark, one of the oldest mints in the Americas.

story: This 1893 eight doubles coin from Guernsey is the oldest coin in this batch, struck during Queen Victoria's reign, though Guernsey's coins show no royal portrait and instead feature the island's shield with three lions from its Norman past and a sprig of leaves. The double was Guernsey's own Channel Islands currency counted eight to a British penny, so this large bronze piece matched the size of a penny, and Guernsey kept its doubles for a century before adopting the pound in full. It is the first coin from Guernsey in the collection. This piece shows plenty of age, with dark toning, smooth wear in places, and pale corrosion spots on the shield side.

The collection already holds a 2004 strike of this coin recorded earlier from a shorthand note; this is the first one photographed on both sides.

story: An Australian 50 cents from 1977, struck for Queen Elizabeth the Second's Silver Jubilee — twenty-five years on the throne. It is a big twelve-sided coin. The front shows the young Queen in Arnold Machin's famous portrait, the one Australia used through the sixties and seventies. The back is a celebration wreath: a shining starburst in the middle ringed by small emblems, with the words SILVER JUBILEE and 50 CENTS around them. It was designed by Stuart Devlin, the goldsmith behind most of Australia's first decimal coins, and it was made to be kept — but plenty slipped into change anyway.

story: A big bronze ten centimes from the France of Napoleon the Third, dated 1867 — three years before his empire collapsed in the Franco-Prussian War. One side carries the Emperor's head wreathed in laurel, ringed by his name and title; the other shows the imperial eagle standing on a thunderbolt, the emblem Napoleon's regiments had carried into battle, with EMPIRE FRANCAIS above and DIX CENTIMES below between two stars. These heavy bronze pieces were the workhorse small change of France for decades — struck in the tens of millions, they stayed in pockets and tills into the next century, which is why so many survive as worn as this one.

story: One of Mexico's best-loved coin designs, struck in bronze from 1943: the Pyramid of the Sun at Teotihuacan fills the reverse, its name carved at the pyramid's base, with the twin volcanoes Iztaccihuatl and Popocatepetl smoking behind it and a radiant Liberty cap dividing the big 20 overhead. Mexico authorized the type in August 1943, in the middle of the Second World War, to replace the silver twenty centavos it could no longer afford to strike - this is a first-year piece, one of some 46 million poured out that year. The obverse carries the national arms, the eagle on its cactus with the snake, and the words ESTADOS UNIDOS MEXICANOS.

story: A two rupees from the India of 2014, part of the series launched in 2011 to carry the rupee's new symbol - the sign that blends the Latin R with the Devanagari RA, adopted in 2010 to give the currency a mark of its own like the dollar or the pound. It sits above the big 2, with lotus flowers curling up both sides. The other face carries the Lion Capital of Ashoka, the four lions of the emperor's pillar that India took as its state emblem, with the country's name in Hindi on the left and English on the right and the motto Truth Alone Triumphs beneath. The small dot under the date marks it as a product of the Noida mint, outside Delhi.
